# Best AI Audio Tools for Podcast Editors in 2026

As a podcast editor, the edit itself is rarely the slow part — transcription, cleanup, filler removal, and level balancing are. The decision you face in 2026 is which of those steps to hand to AI, because the tools divide cleanly by job: recording, cleanup, editing, voiceover, and publishing. This guide walks through the strong candidates and, more importantly, where each one falls short.

## Descript: edit audio like a document

[[link:/tools/79|Descript]] is Freemium and the default recommendation for most editors, because it transcribes your episode and lets you edit by deleting words in the transcript. Cut a rambling sentence by deleting its text; the audio follows. Its use cases are exactly the editor's daily list: podcast editing, video narration, and screen recordings. Two honest limits: some users need a VPN to access the service reliably, and complex music or multitrack editing may suit traditional DAWs better. Descript is superb for spoken-word content; do not expect it to replace a DAW for a produced music bed.

## Auphonic: leveling and noise reduction

[[link:/tools/225|Auphonic]] is Freemium and does one thing very well — podcast polish, loudness compliance, and audio restoration. Run your mixed episode through it and it evens levels and removes noise. The trade-offs: the free tier caps processing time per month for longer episodes, and because processing happens in the cloud you upload audio before hearing any results. For a weekly show, plan around the cap.

## Adobe Podcast AI: fast cleanup

[[link:/tools/1535|Adobe Podcast AI]] is Freemium and aimed at podcast cleanup, voiceovers, and transcription. It is a good complement when you receive guest audio recorded in a hotel room. Pair it with the caution that applies to every cleanup tool: it fixes recording problems, not creative ones, and the free tier has limits.

## ElevenLabs: voiceover and narration

[[link:/tools/8|ElevenLabs]] is Freemium and covers audiobook narration, game character voices, and content localization. Editors use it for intros, stings, and re-voiced lines when a guest mispronounces a name. Be clear-eyed: the free tier is limited and serious production requires a paid plan, and access requires a VPN in some regions, which complicates consistent use.

## Krisp: noise removal at the source

[[link:/tools/1369|Krisp]] is Freemium and removes background noise during calls and recordings — meeting clarity, recording cleanup, and echo removal. It is most valuable during remote recording, before the audio ever reaches your editor. Its limit: very loud or chaotic noise can still leak through the filter, so it reduces problems rather than erasing them.

## Riverside: remote recording

[[link:/tools/1549|Riverside]] is Freemium and handles remote podcast recording, interview capture, and clip repurposing. Editors who also book guests appreciate local recording, which avoids the compression that video-call audio suffers. Caveats: the free plan limits recording hours and video resolution, and remote recording needs good internet and a quiet room.

## Podcastle and Alitu: two more workflows

[[link:/tools/228|Podcastle]] is Freemium for remote recording, AI editing, and voiceover segments — heavy editing sessions can strain older computers and browsers, and the free tier caps recording time and AI features. [[link:/tools/229|Alitu]] is Paid and automates episode publishing, audio cleanup, and show setup; there is no free tier, so you pay before testing the workflow.

## How to choose

If you edit spoken-word shows, Descript plus Auphonic covers 80 percent of the job. If guests record remotely, add Krisp or Riverside at the source. If you need voiceover work, ElevenLabs is the quality pick but budget for its paid plan. If you hate publishing admin, Alitu automates it — but only test it if you are sure you will keep publishing.

## A workflow that chains them

1. Record with Riverside or Podcastle.
2. Remove noise with Krisp at the source or Auphonic after.
3. Transcribe and cut in Descript.
4. Level the mix with Auphonic.
5. Add intros with ElevenLabs; publish with Alitu or your host.

## Common mistakes

Trusting AI cleanup to fix a bad room; ignoring free-tier caps until an episode deadline; multitrack-editing music in Descript when a DAW is the right tool; and assuming every tool works without a VPN in your region.

## FAQ

**Is Descript enough for a full edit?** For spoken-word podcasts, usually yes; music-heavy shows still need a DAW.

**Which tool removes the most noise?** Krisp at recording time, then Auphonic for post polish.

**Can AI do the whole edit unattended?** No — Descript's own docs note complex multitrack work suits traditional DAWs better.

**What about free tiers?** They cap processing time or features; weekly shows usually hit them.
tldr: For spoken-word shows, Descript plus Auphonic covers most of the edit; add Krisp or Riverside for remote guests and ElevenLabs for voiceover work.
